qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ESN) Subject:

Following the mass entry of migrants into Ceuta on 30-31 July 2026, Commission Executive Vice-President Virkkunen stated on 7 August – while organisers and circumstances remained unknown – that Meta and TikTok must act decisively, increase monitoring and strengthen cooperation with fact-checkers1. On 10 August, she announced Digital Services Act-linked crisis protocols and an ad hoc fact-checking mechanism to ‘stifle criminal networks selling false promises’2. Spain’s National Centre for Immigration and Borders.(CENIF) did not submit its report to the Audiencia Nacional until 31 August 2026 (made public on 1 September)3. It describes a sophisticated, planned operation, highlights permissiveness and active guidance by Moroccan security forces, excludes local criminal organisations as capable organisers and does not identify those ultimately responsible for directing the operation4. Social media was therefore an instrument used by third parties, while the facts needed to assess contemporaneous claims only emerged weeks later. 1.

What evidence did the Commission have at the time concerning Meta’s and TikTok’s conduct, as distinct from that of users or organisers, and, if it had none, why did it publicly demand increased monitoring and fact-checking?
Which specific claims were classified as false, and on what contemporaneous evidence, and were any subsequently confirmed or materially qualified by the CENIF report?

Regarding the Commission-coordinated mechanism, what content or accounts were flagged, on what legal basis and with what moderation outcome, and will the Commission publish this audit trail and safeguards protecting lawful or subsequently verified information?

Henna Virkkunen, statement on X, 7 August 2026, https://x.com/HennaVirkkunen/status/2085807830074904693. 2 Henna Virkkunen, statements on X, 10 August 2026, concerning the crisis protocols and fact-checking mechanism and the stated aim of ‘stifling criminal networks’ https://x.com/HennaVirkkunen/status/2086905875889832362 and https://x.com/HennaVirkkunen/status/2086905877433389465. 3 El Español, 1 September 2026, https://www.elespanol.com/espana/tribunales/20260901/policiainforma-juez-invasion-ceuta-guiada-gendarmes-marroquies-ordenes-agentes-paisano-fin-distintomigratorio/1003744369590_0.html. 4 Spanish National Police/CENIF, Report on the irregular mass entry into Ceuta, particularly pp. 10, 16– 17, 34 and 47–50; see also the detailed account in El País, 2 September 2026, https://elpais.com/espana/2026-0902/el-informe-de-la-policia-apunta-que-agentes-marroquies-guiaron-la-entrada-de-migrantes-a-ceuta.html. 1
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.11.2026) The Commission took concrete steps in response to the events in Ceuta. With respect to the role of social media platforms, the Commission acted under the Digital Services Act (DSA)1. Following public reports from civil society organisations early August 2026 on the situation and the related online spread of disinformation capable of inciting violence or endangering people in and around Ceuta2, the Commission asked relevant signatories, including platforms and independent fact-checkers, of the DSA Code of Conduct on Disinformation3 to cooperate in order to establish a direct communication channel through which they could swiftly exchange on harmful disinformation. TikTok, Meta and independent fact-checkers established an enhanced cooperation mechanism on an ad hoc and voluntary basis. Participants have published information in the Code Transparency Centre4. The Commission also closely cooperated with the Spanish Digital Services Coordinator. The Code is a voluntary instrument, and participation is at stakeholders’ discretion. Signatories may withdraw at any time. Information exchanges and moderation decisions remain entirely with participants to the mechanism. The Commission does not have access to content exchanged within the mechanism. Under the Democracy Shield5, strengthening situational awareness and supporting independent fact-checkers, information integrity researchers and civil society organisations is crucial for detecting and monitoring disinformation campaigns, especially in crises. Among other actions, the Commission is developing a DSA incident and crisis response framework to improve preparedness for future cases. Signatories of the Code are also establishing a rapid response system for crises.
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single

Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act), https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng. 2 Including from signatories of the DSA Code of Conduct on Disinformation such as European Fact-checking Standard Network, Newtral and Maldita.es. 3 The Code of Conduct on Disinformation, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/code-conductdisinformation. 4 https://disinfocode.eu/the-code. 5 Joint communication to the European parliament, the council, the European economic and social committee and the Committee of the regions European Democracy Shield: Empowering Strong and Resilient Democracies, JOIN/2025/791 final, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025JC0791.
